articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Question: Where the Tourist Tax Money Actually Goes
articles.dek: Bed tax collections hit record highs last fiscal year. A Flightline review of spending reports shows most dollars never leave the beach — while mainland attractions scramble for scraps.
brief: Escambia County collected $47.2 million in tourist development tax revenue in fiscal year 2025, a 12% increase over the previous year
Roughly 78% of discretionary spending went to Pensacola Beach infrastructure, marketing and events, according to county expenditure reports
Mainland attractions including the National Naval Aviation Museum and Historic Pensacola Village received less than 8% of total allocations
articles.body:
The billboard on I-10 westbound near the Alabama line promises white sand and emerald water. It cost $84,000 for a six-month run. The money came from the same pot that funds lifeguard stands, beach renourishment and the Sea Turtle program — Escambia County's tourist development tax.

Last fiscal year, that pot overflowed. Hotels, vacation rentals and short-term stays generated $47.2 million in bed tax revenue, according to county financial reports obtained by The Flightline. It was the highest collection on record, up 12% from fiscal 2024 and nearly double the $24.8 million collected a decade ago.

The question isn't whether the money is coming in. It's where the money goes out.

Following the dollars

Florida law restricts how counties can spend tourist development tax revenue. The broad categories include tourism promotion, beach and shoreline maintenance, convention facilities and cultural venues. Within those guardrails, county commissioners and the Tourist Development Council have wide discretion.

A Flightline review of expenditure reports, TDC meeting minutes and county budget documents from fiscal years 2023 through 2025 found a consistent pattern: Pensacola Beach dominates the spending.

Of the $38.6 million in discretionary expenditures last fiscal year — money not locked into debt service or state-mandated reserves — approximately $30.1 million went to beach-related projects. That's 78 cents of every discretionary dollar.

The category includes:

  • $8.4 million for beach renourishment projects
  • $6.2 million for Visit Pensacola marketing, which promotes the beach as its primary asset
  • $4.1 million for Pensacola Beach infrastructure including parking, restrooms and the trolley system
  • $3.8 million for beach events and festivals
  • $2.9 million for the Gulf Islands National Seashore partnership agreement
  • $4.7 million for various smaller beach-focused initiatives

County officials defend the allocation as logical.

"The beach is what brings people here," said Escambia County Tourist Development Director Marcus Collinsworth at a March TDC meeting. "You invest in your core product."

Mainland gets the margins

Historic Pensacola Village, operated by the University of West Florida, received $312,000 in TDC funds last fiscal year. The National Naval Aviation Museum — one of the most-visited attractions in Florida — received $485,000 for marketing support.

Combined, those two institutions drew more than 1.2 million visitors in 2025, according to their own attendance figures. They received roughly 2% of discretionary tourist tax spending.

The Pensacola Museum of Art got $89,000. The Pensacola Symphony received $45,000. The Foo Foo Festival, a week-long arts celebration downtown, received $175,000.

Total mainland cultural funding: approximately $2.9 million, or about 7.5% of discretionary spending.

"We're grateful for what we get," said one downtown cultural organization director who asked not to be named because their group applies for TDC grants annually. "But there's a reason we're always scrambling. The pie gets sliced before we even get to the table."

The structure of the split

Escambia County's five-cent tourist development tax breaks down by statute and local ordinance:

  • One cent goes to the Escambia County Marine Resources Division
  • One cent services debt on the Pensacola Bay Center
  • Three cents flow to the general tourist development fund

The TDC, a 12-member advisory board appointed by county commissioners, makes recommendations on how to spend the general fund portion. The Board of County Commissioners has final approval.

Seven of the 12 TDC members have direct business interests on Pensacola Beach — hotels, restaurants or vacation rental companies. That composition is not unusual for tourist development councils statewide, but critics say it shapes priorities.

"The people making recommendations are the people who benefit most from beach spending," said Pensacola City Council member Tenley Morrison at an April joint meeting with county officials. "I'm not saying it's corrupt. I'm saying it's structural."

County Commissioner Lumon May, who represents mainland District 3, has raised similar concerns.

"My constituents pay into this tax when they stay at hotels downtown or on the north end," May said in an interview. "They should see some return. Right now, the math doesn't work for them."

The beach argument

Defenders of the current allocation point to economics. Pensacola Beach generates the largest share of hotel room nights in the county. More than 60% of bed tax revenue comes from beach properties, according to county estimates.

"The beach pays in, the beach gets invested in," said Sarah Linderman, general manager of a Pensacola Beach resort and TDC member. "That's not favoritism. That's proportionality."

Beach advocates also note that renourishment and infrastructure serve the entire county's tourism brand.

"When someone sees our beach on Instagram, they might stay downtown," Collinsworth said. "It's all connected."

But the connection runs thinner the farther from the water you get. Hotels in downtown Pensacola and along the Scenic Highway corridor report that visitors often don't realize there are things to do beyond the beach.

"People check in and ask where the beach shuttle is," said a manager at a downtown boutique hotel. "They didn't come for the museums. They came for the beach and booked cheaper rooms over here."

What changes look like

Some Florida counties with similar tourism profiles have experimented with different models.

In Bay County, home to Panama City Beach, the TDC allocates a fixed percentage — currently 15% — for cultural and heritage tourism distinct from beach marketing. Okaloosa County created a separate grant program for mainland attractions with its own dedicated funding stream.

Escambia County has no such carve-out. Mainland attractions compete in the same grant pool as beach events, often losing to projects with more direct visitor impact metrics.

Commissioner May has proposed creating a mainland tourism subcommittee with dedicated funding. The idea has not gained traction.

"We're not there yet," said Commission Chair Jeff Bergosh. "But I think the conversation is worth having."

The bottom line

Escambia County's tourist tax generates more revenue than ever. The beach remains the economic engine. And mainland attractions — the history, the culture, the institutions that give Pensacola a story beyond white sand — continue to operate on what's left over.

Whether that's sound strategy or structural neglect depends on where you sit. At the Pensacola Beach Boardwalk, the money is visible: new restrooms, replenished dunes, packed parking lots. At the T.T. Wentworth museum downtown, the roof still leaks.

The tourist tax doesn't fix roofs. It markets what's already shining.

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: The Warehouse District's Quiet Transformation
articles.dek: Between the railroad tracks and Main Street, a dozen properties have changed hands in 18 months. Who's buying, what they're planning, and why city hall isn't talking about it.
brief: At least 12 commercial properties in Pensacola's Warehouse District have sold since January 2025, totaling more than $14 million in transactions according to Escambia County property records.
Several purchases trace back to three LLCs registered in Delaware with no apparent local connection, though two share a registered agent with developments in Nashville and Austin.
City planning staff confirmed no major rezoning applications have been filed for the area, and council members contacted by The Flightline said they were unaware of any coordinated development plans.
articles.body:
The loading dock at 412 West Intendencia Street still holds pallets of ceramic tile. A forklift sits where someone left it in March, keys dangling from the ignition. But the company that operated here for 31 years is gone. The building sold in February to an entity called Harbor Light Holdings LLC for $1.2 million—three times what it appraised for in 2023.

This is one transaction. There have been at least eleven others like it.

Between January 2025 and last month, a stretch of the Warehouse District running from Tarragona Street to the CSX tracks has seen more ownership turnover than in the previous decade combined. The buyers are mostly LLCs. The sellers are mostly longtime operators or their estates. The prices are consistently above market.

And nobody at city hall seems to know what's coming next.

Following the paper trail

Escambia County property records show 12 commercial sales in the district since the start of 2025. The Flightline verified each through the county property appraiser's office and cross-referenced with Florida Division of Corporations filings.

Three LLCs account for seven of the purchases: Harbor Light Holdings, Meridian South Partners, and Gulf Standard Development. All three are registered in Delaware. Florida corporate filings list a Tallahassee law firm as their registered agent—the same firm that handles filings for development groups active in Nashville's Gulch district and Austin's East Side.

The connection doesn't prove coordination. But it suggests these aren't local investors picking up opportunistic deals.

"When you see Delaware LLCs using the same registered agent buying contiguous properties over a short window, that's a pattern," said Marcus Whitfield, a commercial real estate attorney in Mobile who reviewed the filings at The Flightline's request. "Could be coincidence. Usually isn't."

The remaining five properties sold to a mix of buyers: two to a Pensacola-based investor who owns several downtown buildings, one to an out-of-state family trust, and two to LLCs that trace back to a Birmingham investment group.

What the buildings are

The Warehouse District isn't zoned for residential use. It's a patchwork of light industrial, commercial, and mixed-use designations that date back to the 1980s when the city last updated its comprehensive plan for the area.

The buildings themselves are mostly single-story masonry structures from the 1940s through 1970s. High ceilings. Concrete floors. Large footprints. The kind of bones that developers in other cities have converted into breweries, food halls, creative offices, and loft apartments.

Currently, the district houses building supply companies, a commercial printer, two auto repair shops, a welding operation, and several buildings that appear vacant. The tile distributor at 412 West Intendencia was among the last active wholesale operations.

Maria Santos ran the office there for 22 years. She found out about the sale two weeks before it closed.

"They told us the new owners had other plans," Santos said. "Nobody told us what the plans were. We just got our last checks and that was it."

The silence from city hall

Pensacola's planning department confirmed that no rezoning applications, site plans, or development permits have been filed for any of the 12 properties. Planning Director Jennifer Crockett said her office has not received any pre-application inquiries either.

"We track those informally," Crockett said. "Nothing's come across my desk for that area."

Three City Council members—Andy Terhaar, Teniadé Broughton, and Allison Patton—responded to requests for comment. None said they had been briefed on any development plans for the Warehouse District. Terhaar represents the district where most of the properties sit.

"This is news to me," Terhaar said. "I'm interested to learn more about what you've found."

Mayor D.C. Reeves' office did not respond to two emails and a phone message seeking comment.

The lack of official filings doesn't mean nothing is planned. Developers routinely acquire properties before engaging with municipal planning processes. In some cases, they wait years.

But the volume and pace of these sales—plus the apparent out-of-state coordination—has caught the attention of some who work in the area.

Watching from next door

Raymond Oates has operated Gulf Coast Welding & Fabrication on West Government Street for 19 years. His building isn't among the sold properties. Not yet.

"I've had three people reach out in the last six months asking if I want to sell," Oates said. "I told them I'm not interested. They keep calling."

He said the callers identified themselves as representatives of investment groups but declined to name the groups or say what they planned to do with properties they acquired.

"One guy told me the area was going to change whether I liked it or not," Oates said. "I asked him what that meant. He just said I should think about my options."

Oates said he doesn't oppose development. He said he opposes being kept in the dark.

"If somebody's got a plan for this neighborhood, tell us what it is," he said. "Let us be part of the conversation. Don't just show up one day with bulldozers."

What could be coming

Without official filings or statements from the buyers, any discussion of future plans is speculation. But the physical characteristics of the district—and its location—offer clues about what might make economic sense.

The Warehouse District sits between downtown Pensacola's commercial core and the waterfront. It's less than a mile from Palafox Street. The CSX rail line that borders it has been discussed for years as a potential route for commuter rail or a linear park, though no concrete plans have materialized.

Similar districts in peer cities have become targets for mixed-use redevelopment. The Gulch in Nashville. The Bottleworks District in Indianapolis. Houston's East End. The playbook is familiar: acquire undervalued industrial properties, wait for or encourage zoning changes, then develop residential, retail, and office space marketed to young professionals.

Whether that model works in Pensacola—a smaller market with different demographics and growth patterns—is an open question.

"Pensacola's not Nashville," said Dr. Carolyn Meadows, an urban planning professor at the University of West Florida. "The demand drivers are different. The capital markets are different. That doesn't mean this kind of development can't happen here. It means the economics have to make sense for this specific place."

Meadows said she was not aware of the property transfers until contacted by The Flightline.

What happens next

The new owners have options. They can hold the properties and wait. They can lease them to existing industrial users. They can seek rezoning and pursue development. They can sell to someone else.

What they can't do—at least not indefinitely—is avoid public scrutiny if they want to build anything significant. Florida's Sunshine Laws require public notice for rezoning hearings. Site plans for commercial development are public records. Environmental assessments, traffic studies, utility impact analyses—all of these generate paper trails that residents can access and challenge.

For now, the paper trail is thin. Deeds have been recorded. LLCs have been registered. Money has changed hands.

The forklift at 412 West Intendencia still has its keys in the ignition. But the building belongs to someone else now. Someone who hasn't said what they want to do with it.

That silence is a choice. It's also temporary. Eventually, plans require permits. Permits require applications. Applications become public.

The Flightline will be watching when they do.

This story will be updated as new information becomes available. If you have knowledge of development plans in the Warehouse District, contact our newsroom.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's Hurricane Season Prep Includes New Evacuation Protocol for Training Squadrons
articles.dek: After lessons learned from recent storms, the base will move aircraft earlier and faster this year. For the 800-plus student aviators cycling through, that means schedule disruptions are now baked into the calendar.
brief: Naval Air Station Pensacola will begin aircraft evacuations 96 hours before projected tropical storm conditions, up from the previous 72-hour threshold
The new protocol affects Training Air Wing Six and visiting squadrons, with pre-designated evacuation routes to bases in Texas, Mississippi, and Georgia
Student naval aviators will see built-in schedule buffers of up to two weeks during peak hurricane season to account for potential disruptions
articles.body:
The T-6B Texan II trainers sit in neat rows on the flight line at Sherman Field, their orange and white paint schemes bright against the tarmac. By August, many of them could be 400 miles away in Corpus Christi or Meridian, parked there because of a storm that hasn't formed yet.

That's the new math at Naval Air Station Pensacola. Base leadership announced this week that hurricane evacuation protocols for training aircraft will trigger a full day earlier than in previous years—96 hours before projected tropical storm conditions instead of 72.

"We're not going to get caught flat-footed again," said Capt. Timothy Kinsella, NAS Pensacola's commanding officer, during a briefing Thursday. "The 2024 and 2025 seasons taught us that waiting for certainty means you've already waited too long."

The cost of close calls

The change follows two consecutive hurricane seasons that tested the base's readiness. In September 2024, Hurricane Helene's wobbling track forced a compressed 48-hour evacuation of training aircraft when the storm's projected path shifted east. Maintenance crews worked through the night. Two aircraft remained on deck when the decision was made to shelter in place.

Last year, a late-season system that never made landfall still generated tropical storm conditions over Pensacola Bay, grounding training flights for six days.

Neither event caused significant damage. But both revealed gaps.

"Every hour we spend scrambling is an hour we're not training pilots," Kinsella said. "The irony is that being more conservative with evacuations actually protects the flight schedule."

What changes for student aviators

NAS Pensacola processes roughly 800 student naval aviators annually through primary flight training. They arrive from Officer Candidate School and the Naval Academy on fixed schedules, compete for limited flight hours, and face pressure to complete syllabi on time.

Hurricane disruptions have historically created cascading delays. A week of lost training can push graduation dates, affect follow-on school assignments, and create bottlenecks in the training pipeline.

Under the new protocol, the Training Air Wing Six schedule will include built-in buffer periods during peak hurricane season—roughly August 15 through October 15. Students arriving during those windows will see syllabi that account for up to two weeks of potential weather disruption.

"It's about setting realistic expectations," said Cmdr. Rachel Ostrowski, Training Air Wing Six's operations officer. "We're not adding time to the program. We're acknowledging that the time was always at risk."

The buffers apply to primary training squadrons VT-2, VT-3, and VT-6. Advanced training conducted at other installations follows separate protocols.

Evacuation logistics

Pre-positioned evacuation plans now designate specific routes and receiving bases for different aircraft types:

  • T-6B trainers will evacuate primarily to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi in Texas and Naval Air Station Meridian in Mississippi
  • Transient aircraft and administrative planes will route to Dobbins Air Reserve Base in Georgia
  • Helicopters assigned to search and rescue will shelter at Whiting Field in Milton or evacuate to New Orleans depending on storm track

The 96-hour trigger applies when the National Hurricane Center's forecast cone includes Pensacola at tropical storm strength or higher. Evacuation authority rests with the installation commander, though coordination with Commander, Naval Air Forces will occur for any movement involving more than 20 aircraft.

Ground support equipment, maintenance records, and essential personnel will move in phases. Non-essential personnel will follow Escambia County evacuation orders.

Coordination with Whiting Field

Naval Air Station Whiting Field in Milton, 25 miles north of Pensacola, operates under a separate command but coordinates closely on hurricane response. The two installations share weather resources and evacuation planning.

Whiting Field's TH-73A helicopters and fixed-wing trainers follow similar protocols, though the base's inland location provides marginally more shelter from storm surge. Whiting's aircraft may shelter in place for systems that primarily threaten coastal areas.

"We talk daily during hurricane season," said Lt. Cmdr. James Polk, NAS Pensacola's emergency management officer. "Different geography, same mission. We can't have one base evacuating while the other waits."

Community impact

Aircraft evacuations are visible events. Residents near the base notice when the flight line empties. Local businesses that serve military families see spending patterns shift when training pauses.

The earlier trigger means evacuations may occur for storms that ultimately miss the area or weaken before arrival. Kinsella acknowledged the potential for what he called "false positive" evacuations but argued the cost is acceptable.

"I'd rather explain why we moved aircraft for a storm that didn't hit than explain why we didn't move them for one that did," he said.

Hurricane season officially begins June 1. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast an above-average season for the Gulf of Mexico, with 18 to 22 named storms predicted basin-wide.

NAS Pensacola will hold its annual hurricane exercise June 12, testing the new protocols with a simulated Category 2 storm scenario.
